title: The Trigger, Not the Threshold: What Actually Gets an Owner to Call a Fractional CFO
excerpt: Most owners don't bring in extra financial support because revenue hit a certain number. They bring it in because of a specific moment. Here are the three that come up most often.
content:
Ask most owners when they decided to bring in extra financial support and very few describe a plan. Fewer still describe a revenue figure. What they usually describe is a moment: a question from a bank they couldn't answer with confidence, a decision made on gut feel because there was no time to model it properly, a quiet unease that the numbers looked fine and something still felt off.

There is a lot of talk about readiness in terms of size, whether a business has crossed a million dollars in revenue or built out a certain headcount. Size is a reasonable proxy for complexity, and it is a fine starting point for a conversation about what a fractional CFO actually does. But it rarely predicts the actual day someone picks up the phone. The trigger does that, and across the owner-led businesses we work with along the East Coast, the trigger is almost never about size at all.

Three moments come up more often than any others.

A lender asks a question the business can't answer with confidence

It usually happens during a facility increase or a refinance. The bank doesn't just want last year's financials, it wants a forward view: what does cash look like over the next quarter, under more than one scenario, and what happens to serviceability if trade slows. For a lot of owner-led businesses, this is the first time anyone has actually asked for a forward number rather than a historical one, and the gap shows up fast. The reporting has been accurate the whole time. It was simply never built to look ahead, which is a different job to the one ongoing cash flow discipline is designed to solve. Owners in this position often describe the same feeling, that they know the business well but were suddenly asked a question about it they had never had to answer out loud before.

Growth starts outrunning the reporting

Revenue is climbing, the team is growing, and the monthly numbers still arrive on the same lag they always have. Nothing has technically gone wrong. But the owner can feel the read slipping, a sense that the bank balance and what the ledger says are drifting apart, or that the margin on this year's growth hasn't actually been checked against last year's. Your bookkeeper is doing exactly what they should be doing, keeping the ledger accurate and current, because that is the job. What most bookkeeping arrangements are not built for is translating that ledger into a forward-looking read the owner can act on week to week, and growth is usually what exposes that gap first, simply because there is more happening for the reporting to fall behind.

A decision bigger than the usual ones is on the table

An acquisition opportunity, a capital raise, a large lease commitment, a senior hire, or an unsolicited approach from a buyer. These decisions do not arrive often, which is exactly the problem: most owners have never made one before and are not going to get a second attempt at making it well. This is the moment owners most often want someone at the table who has structured this kind of decision before, rather than someone who produces the numbers after the decision has already been made. It is also where a fractional CFO partnership earns its place fastest, because the value shows up in the decision itself, not just in the reporting that follows it.

Why the trigger matters more than the timing

None of these three moments arrive on a schedule, and waiting for a tidier, more convenient version of the business to show up first usually just means the moment gets managed alone, under pressure, with whatever information happens to be on hand at the time. That is precisely why fractional support is structured in tiers rather than offered as a single fixed package, so the level of involvement can match what is actually happening in the business right now rather than a revenue bracket it happened to cross at some earlier point.

If one of these three moments sounds like a conversation you've had recently, with a bank, with yourself late on a Sunday night, or with a decision that is still sitting unresolved on your desk, that is usually a better signal than any number on the P&L. It is also a reasonable enough reason to book a discovery call and talk through what level of support would actually fit, rather than waiting for a size that never quite feels like the right one.

faqs.q: How do I know if my business is ready for a fractional CFO?
faqs.a: Readiness is less about a specific revenue figure and more about pattern recognition, a lender asking a forward-looking question you can't confidently answer, growth outrunning your reporting, or a major decision on the table with no one to pressure-test it. This guide on what a fractional CFO actually does is a useful starting point.

faqs.q: What does a fractional CFO cost for an Australian SME?
faqs.a: Cost depends on the tier of involvement, from a monthly management pack through to weekly involvement in leadership, lender and board conversations, and it scales with what the business actually needs rather than a single fixed rate. This guide to fractional CFO cost breaks down how the tiers are typically structured and priced, so you can gauge roughly where your business would sit before the first conversation.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a bookkeeper, an accountant and a fractional CFO?
faqs.a: A bookkeeper and BAS agent keep the ledger accurate, current and compliant. An accountant handles lodgements, tax structure and the annual compliance calendar. A fractional CFO sits on top of both, turning that accurate historical data into forward decisions about cash, margin, pricing and growth. All three roles work alongside each other, not in competition, and a well-run business genuinely needs all three.

faqs.q: Can a fractional CFO help with a bank facility or refinance?
faqs.a: Yes, this is one of the most common moments a fractional CFO gets brought in. Lenders increasingly want a forward cash flow scenario rather than historical financials alone, and building a credible one under time pressure is exactly the kind of gap fractional support is designed to close, alongside a proper banking and facility review of what is actually on offer.

faqs.q: Is a fractional CFO only useful for businesses about to raise capital or sell?
faqs.a: No, most engagements are ongoing monthly support rather than transaction-driven. That said, an active raise or sale does change the workload noticeably, which is why capital raise support is typically layered on top of an existing partnership for the duration of the transaction, rather than treated as a separate, standalone engagement from scratch.

faqs.q: How many hours a week does a fractional CFO typically work?
faqs.a: It varies by tier, from a monthly cadence focused on reporting and forecasting through to weekly involvement in leadership, lender and board conversations for businesses moving through a more demanding period. There is no single answer, because the right level of hours is decided by what the business needs that month, not a fixed roster. Current tiers and what each one includes are set out on the pricing page.

faqs.q: Do I need to wait for a certain size before hiring a fractional CFO?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Size is a reasonable proxy for complexity, but the more reliable signal is usually a specific trigger: a lender's question you couldn't confidently answer, a decision bigger than the usual ones, or reporting that has quietly stopped keeping pace with growth, rather than a revenue figure marked on a calendar somewhere.
